narrative:
The model determined that you have an 80.5% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is so high, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors from your academic record. Your first-year and third-year class rankings were by far the strongest reasons the model predicted failure. Both placed you in the bottom decile of your school, far below the average of roughly sixth decile among students who were accepted. These unusually low rankings strongly pushed the prediction toward bar exam failure. Your undergraduate GPA of 2.8 also worked against you, though its influence was smaller; it sits noticeably below the 3.23 average of accepted students and therefore added a modest additional push toward failure.

Your LSAT score of 31, upper-middle family income, and plan to attend full-time had far less impact on the outcome. The model focused overwhelmingly on your school performance rather than these other details.

To improve your chances, you should focus on raising your academic performance to the middle of your class or higher before reapplying, or consider retaking the LSAT to demonstrate stronger readiness. Many students strengthen their profiles this way and succeed on a second attempt.
